questions.stem: What was the most serious human consequence of the Great Leap Forward?
options: a war with the Soviet Union along the northern border in 1960
the forced migration of all city workers to the countryside
a rapid rise in food exports that made China a rich country
a famine in 1959-1961 in which millions of people died
questions.explanation: Unrealistic targets, false reports, grain procurement and the disruption of farming caused a catastrophic famine; estimates of the deaths vary widely but run into the tens of millions. Border clashes with the USSR came in 1969.

questions.stem: How did the failure of the Great Leap Forward change Mao's position in the early 1960s?
options: He gained total control and removed Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping from office in 1960
He resigned as party chairman and handed the post to Zhou Enlai at the Lushan Conference
He stepped back from day-to-day policy while Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping led the recovery
He was expelled from the Communist Party and lived in exile in the Soviet Union until 1966
questions.explanation: Mao gave up the post of head of state to Liu Shaoqi in 1959 and withdrew to the 'second line', while Liu and Deng restored private plots and material incentives. Mao remained party chairman and came to resent their policies.

questions.stem: Why did Mao come to see Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping as a threat by the mid-1960s?
options: He believed they planned to hand the economy over to the United States in return for food aid
He believed they wanted to restart the Great Leap Forward, which he had decided to abandon
He believed they had secretly arranged for the Nationalists to return to power from Taiwan
He believed their pragmatic recovery policies were taking China down a 'capitalist road' like Soviet revisionism
questions.explanation: Mao feared that bureaucrats and material incentives would recreate a privileged elite, as he believed had happened in Khrushchev's USSR. Liu and Deng had overseen the retreat from the Great Leap, not its revival.

questions.stem: In November 1965 Yao Wenyuan published an attack on Wu Han's play Hai Rui Dismissed from Office. Why is this seen as an opening shot of the Cultural Revolution?
options: The play had been written by Mao himself, so attacking it showed Yao's independence
The play called for Western democracy, so it had already been banned by the Politburo
The play was read as a defence of Peng Dehuai, so attacking it targeted Mao's critics in the party
The play praised the Gang of Four, so attacking it was a way of criticising Jiang Qing
questions.explanation: The play about an honest Ming official dismissed by the emperor was seen as an allegory of Peng Dehuai's dismissal after Lushan. Wu Han was a deputy mayor of Beijing, so the attack began the move against the Beijing party leadership.

questions.stem: Which was one of Mao's main aims in launching the Cultural Revolution in 1966?
options: to remove 'capitalist roaders' in the party and renew revolutionary spirit among the young
to open China to foreign investment and build closer ties with the United States
to restore the traditional Confucian values that the party had attacked since 1949
to hand power to an elected parliament and allow multiple parties to compete
questions.explanation: Mao wanted to purge leaders he thought were revisionist, reassert his authority and give a new generation the experience of revolution. The campaign attacked Confucian and traditional culture rather than restoring it.

questions.stem: Which method did Mao use to mobilise young people against the party establishment in 1966?
options: He endorsed the Red Guards and received millions of them at mass rallies in Tiananmen Square
He ordered the army to arrest students who criticised party officials in big-character posters
He closed all newspapers and radio stations so that students could hear only foreign broadcasts
He offered students jobs in the Soviet Union if they joined the campaign against the party
questions.explanation: From August 1966 Mao appeared at a series of huge rallies of Red Guards, encouraged them to 'rebel' against authority, and let them travel free across China. The army under Lin Biao supported the campaign.

questions.stem: Which leader, as Minister of Defence, promoted the cult of Mao in the army and was named Mao's successor in 1969?
options: Lin Biao
Zhou Enlai
Hua Guofeng
Zhao Ziyang
questions.explanation: Lin Biao built up the cult of Mao in the People's Liberation Army and was written into the party constitution as successor at the Ninth Congress in 1969. He died in 1971 after an alleged plot against Mao.

questions.stem: The Gang of Four consisted of:
options: Liu Shaoqi, Deng Xiaoping, Peng Zhen and Wu Han
Hua Guofeng, Marshal Ye Jianying, Wang Dongxing and Chen Yun
Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan and Wang Hongwen
Jiang Qing, Lin Biao, Chen Boda and Kang Sheng
questions.explanation: Mao's wife Jiang Qing and three Shanghai radicals formed the core of the radical faction in the later Cultural Revolution. Liu, Deng, Peng Zhen and Wu Han were among their victims, and Hua and Ye arrested them in 1976.

questions.stem: From 1967 the Red Guard movement became a problem for Mao mainly because:
options: rival Red Guard factions fought one another, bringing violent chaos to many cities
the Red Guards refused to read Mao's works and turned instead to studying Western liberal ideas
the Red Guards joined Liu Shaoqi and demanded an end to the Cultural Revolution
the Red Guards seized control of the army and declared a military government
questions.explanation: Factions each claiming to be truly loyal to Mao fought pitched battles, some with weapons seized from the army. From 1968 Mao used the army and worker teams to restore order and sent millions of young people to the countryside.

questions.stem: How did the Gang of Four exercise influence in the early 1970s?
options: through control of the economic ministries, which they used to open China to foreign trade
through alliances with Deng Xiaoping and Zhou Enlai, who shared their political aims
through control of propaganda, culture and the media, and through the radical base in Shanghai
through command of the main army regions, which they used to defeat Lin Biao's supporters in battle
questions.explanation: The radicals dominated the press, the arts and the Shanghai party organisation and used campaigns such as 'Criticise Lin, Criticise Confucius' against Zhou Enlai. They had little support in the army, and they opposed Zhou and Deng.

questions.stem: What was the 'Up to the Mountains and Down to the Countryside' movement from late 1968?
options: sending millions of urban young people to live and work in rural areas
moving the Communist Party headquarters from Beijing to the countryside
building new mountain cities for factories that were safe from nuclear attack
allowing peasants to move freely to the cities to find better-paid work
questions.explanation: Mao's directive sent educated urban youth to villages and remote regions to 'learn from the peasants', which also removed unemployed former Red Guards from the cities. Many spent years there and missed out on education.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the impact of the Cultural Revolution on education?
options: Education was unaffected, because the Cultural Revolution was limited to the party leadership
Schools taught mainly foreign languages to prepare students for work in Western countries
Schools and universities were closed or disrupted, and entrance exams were abolished until 1977
Universities expanded rapidly and admitted students only through highly competitive national exams
questions.explanation: Classes stopped in 1966, teachers were attacked, and when universities reopened from 1970 they admitted 'worker-peasant-soldier' students on political recommendation. National entrance exams returned only in late 1977, after Mao's death.

questions.stem: Under Jiang Qing's direction, cultural life during the Cultural Revolution was dominated by:
options: Western films and novels, imported to show the weaknesses of capitalist societies
local folk festivals that the party encouraged each village to organise freely
a small number of revolutionary 'model works', such as model operas and ballets
a revival of traditional Beijing opera featuring emperors, generals and scholars
questions.explanation: The 'model works' (yangbanxi) presented heroic workers, peasants and soldiers and were among the few performances allowed. Traditional operas about emperors and scholars were condemned as feudal.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the economic impact of the Cultural Revolution?
options: The economy grew faster than at any time since 1949 because of new markets and foreign investment
The economy was untouched because the campaign was confined to culture and the arts
Industry was badly disrupted in 1967-1968, but the damage was less severe than in the Great Leap Forward
The economy collapsed into a famine much worse than the Great Leap Forward famine of 1959-1961
questions.explanation: Factional fighting and strikes cut industrial output in 1967-1968, and planning and transport broke down in places, but output recovered from 1969 and there was no famine on the scale of 1959-1961. Foreign investment came only in the reform era.

questions.stem: During the Cultural Revolution, intellectuals, teachers and former 'class enemies' were often:
options: publicly humiliated at struggle sessions, beaten, imprisoned or sent to labour camps
promoted to senior party posts because their skills were urgently needed
sent abroad to study in the Soviet Union and return as party teachers
left alone, since the campaign targeted only foreigners living in China
questions.explanation: Red Guards targeted people with 'bad' class backgrounds, education or foreign links, and many died or took their own lives. Hundreds of thousands at least died in the violence of the period, though estimates vary.

questions.stem: What happened to Deng Xiaoping during the Cultural Revolution?
options: He led the Red Guards in Beijing and became Mao's chosen successor at the Ninth Congress
He fled to Taiwan in 1967 and returned only after the death of Mao in September 1976
He remained premier throughout the Cultural Revolution and protected Liu Shaoqi
He was purged, sent to work in a tractor factory in Jiangxi, and later restored in 1973
questions.explanation: Deng was denounced as the 'number two capitalist roader' after Liu Shaoqi and sent to Jiangxi. Zhou Enlai helped bring him back as vice-premier in 1973, but he was purged again in April 1976.

questions.stem: Which development best shows the Cultural Revolution's impact on the Communist Party itself?
options: The party gave up its monopoly of power and allowed other parties to contest national elections
The party moved its leadership to Shanghai and gave up all control over the People's Liberation Army
Party committees were overthrown and replaced by revolutionary committees in which the army had a major role
The party grew stronger and more united, with no leading member removed from office at any time during the decade
questions.explanation: Party organisations were paralysed or overthrown in 1967 and replaced by 'three-in-one' revolutionary committees of army officers, cadres and rebels. Many senior leaders were purged, and the army's political role grew until the fall of Lin Biao.

questions.stem: Lin Biao's death in September 1971 after an alleged plot against Mao damaged the Cultural Revolution mainly because:
options: it led the Gang of Four to resign from the Politburo and leave politics completely
it caused the Soviet Union to invade China, which forced Mao to end the campaign at once
Mao's chosen successor was now called a traitor, which deepened public cynicism about the campaign
it ended the army's role in politics, leaving the Red Guards in full control of the party
questions.explanation: Lin had been praised as Mao's closest comrade and written into the party constitution as successor. His sudden disgrace made many Chinese question the official story and the wisdom of the leadership.

questions.stem: Zhou Enlai, who had served as premier since 1949, died in:
options: January 1976
September 1971
October 1977
December 1978
questions.explanation: Zhou died on 8 January 1976. Lin Biao died in 1971, the Eleventh Party Congress declared the Cultural Revolution over in 1977, and the Third Plenum of December 1978 launched Deng's reforms.

questions.stem: In April 1976, during the Qingming festival, crowds in Tiananmen Square:
options: mourned the death of Mao Zedong and swore loyalty to Hua Guofeng as his heir
laid wreaths and poems honouring Zhou Enlai, which also criticised the radicals
celebrated the arrest of the Gang of Four and called for Deng to become premier
demanded multiparty elections and built a statue modelled on the Statue of Liberty
questions.explanation: The mourning for Zhou became an implicit protest against the Gang of Four. The square was cleared by force on 5 April, the event was condemned as counter-revolutionary, and Deng was blamed and removed from his posts.

questions.stem: Why is the Tiananmen Incident of April 1976 significant to the end of the Cultural Revolution?
options: It led directly to Mao's resignation and to free elections for a new party leadership
It brought Deng Xiaoping to power as premier immediately after the crowds in the square had been dispersed
It persuaded Mao to name Jiang Qing as his successor as chairman of the Communist Party
It showed widespread public hostility to the radicals, which later helped justify their arrest
questions.explanation: The protests revealed how unpopular the Gang of Four had become. In the short term Deng was purged and Hua Guofeng was promoted, but in 1978 the incident was officially reclassified as a revolutionary action.

questions.stem: Mao Zedong died in:
options: January 1976
September 1971
April 1969
September 1976
questions.explanation: Mao died on 9 September 1976. Within a month the Gang of Four had been arrested, and the Cultural Revolution was officially declared over in 1977.

questions.stem: How was the Gang of Four removed from power in October 1976?
options: They lost a vote of the Central Committee and resigned peacefully to retire in Shanghai
Red Guards stormed their offices in Beijing and handed them over to the police
Deng Xiaoping led an army revolt from Guangzhou and arrested them in a battle
Hua Guofeng had them arrested with the support of senior military and security leaders
questions.explanation: Hua, Marshal Ye Jianying and Wang Dongxing, commander of the leadership's guard unit, had them arrested on 6 October 1976. They were later blamed for the excesses of the Cultural Revolution and tried in 1980-1981.

questions.stem: At the televised trial of the Gang of Four in 1980-1981, the party mainly sought to:
options: acquit the radicals so that the party could repair relations with Shanghai
blame the radicals for the Cultural Revolution while protecting Mao's overall standing
show that Mao alone had planned every event of the Cultural Revolution
prove that Deng Xiaoping had secretly supported the radicals since 1966
questions.explanation: Jiang Qing and Zhang Chunqiao received death sentences with a reprieve (later commuted). The 1981 party resolution said Mao bore chief responsibility for the Cultural Revolution's errors but that his contributions far outweighed his mistakes.

questions.stem: Hua Guofeng's policy of the 'Two Whatevers' weakened his position against Deng because it:
options: required him to share power with Jiang Qing, who was still popular with the party
bound him to upholding all of Mao's decisions, while Deng argued practice should test truth
committed him to closing the Special Economic Zones that Deng had built in Guangdong
made him promise to restore Lin Biao's reputation and return all of Lin's followers to high office
questions.explanation: Hua's slogan meant following whatever Mao had decided and instructed, which left little room for change. Deng and his allies promoted the idea that 'practice is the sole criterion of truth', which justified reform. The SEZs came after Hua's decline.

questions.stem: The Third Plenum of the Eleventh Central Committee in December 1978 is seen as a turning point because it:
options: restored the Cultural Revolution Group and returned the Gang of Four to power
ended the Communist Party's monopoly of power and legalised opposition parties
shifted the party's focus to economic modernisation and confirmed Deng's leadership
made Deng party chairman and premier at once, and abolished the old Central Committee
questions.explanation: The plenum moved the party away from class struggle towards 'reform and opening', and Deng became the dominant leader. He never took the titles of party chairman or premier, ruling through allies such as Hu Yaobang and Zhao Ziyang.

questions.stem: The Four Modernisations were in:
options: housing, transport, health care, and the arts and traditional culture
agriculture, industry, national defence, and science and technology
agriculture, religion, the legal system, and foreign trade with Japan
industry, democracy, education, and the reform of the Communist Party
questions.explanation: Zhou Enlai first set out the Four Modernisations, and Deng made them the centre of policy after 1978. Democracy was not one of them; Wei Jingsheng called it the missing 'Fifth Modernisation'.

questions.stem: The household responsibility system of the late 1970s and early 1980s allowed peasant families to:
options: join larger people's communes that shared all tools, land and income equally
farm allocated land and sell any surplus above a state quota on the market
own their land outright and sell it to any buyer they chose at market prices
leave farming and move freely to the cities without needing any permission
questions.explanation: Families contracted plots from the collective, delivered a quota to the state and kept or sold the rest. Output rose sharply and the communes were dismantled by the mid-1980s. Land remained collectively owned.

questions.stem: The first Special Economic Zones, created in 1980, included:
options: Yan'an, the wartime base
Shenzhen, next to Hong Kong
Beijing, the national capital
Lhasa, the capital of Tibet
questions.explanation: Shenzhen, Zhuhai and Shantou in Guangdong and Xiamen in Fujian were opened to foreign investment with tax breaks and freer markets. Coastal sites close to Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan were chosen to attract investors.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a social consequence of Deng's economic reforms by the late 1980s?
options: All state enterprises were sold to foreign companies, ending China's state sector
Living standards rose for many, but inflation, corruption and inequality caused discontent
Incomes fell for most people, so the reforms were abandoned and the people's communes restored
Prices were frozen for a decade, so no one in the cities was affected by inflation
questions.explanation: Incomes and consumer goods increased, but price reform in 1988 fuelled high inflation, and officials and their families profited from the dual-track price system. These grievances fed the 1989 protests. Much of industry remained state-owned.

questions.stem: Wei Jingsheng's call for a 'Fifth Modernisation' at the Democracy Wall in 1978 led to:
options: Deng's resignation and the appointment of Wei as general secretary in 1980
his arrest in 1979 and a long prison sentence, as Deng closed the Democracy Wall
his appointment to the Politburo, where he wrote China's new constitution
the immediate holding of free national elections under international supervision
questions.explanation: Deng tolerated the Democracy Wall while it helped him against Hua, but Wei's essay demanding democracy and criticising Deng went too far. Wei was sentenced to fifteen years, and Deng set out the Four Cardinal Principles, including the leadership of the party.

questions.stem: Why was Hu Yaobang forced to resign as general secretary in January 1987?
options: He was found to have plotted with the Gang of Four to restore the Cultural Revolution
Party elders blamed him for being too soft on the student protests of December 1986
He had ordered the army to fire on students in Hefei and Shanghai in December 1986
He opposed the Special Economic Zones and wanted to return to collective agriculture
questions.explanation: Hu was seen as a liberal reformer, and conservatives blamed him for tolerating 'bourgeois liberalisation' when students protested for more freedom. Zhao Ziyang replaced him, and his death in April 1989 triggered the Tiananmen protests.

questions.stem: The Tiananmen Square protests of 1989 began after the death in April of:
options: Zhao Ziyang
Hu Yaobang
Zhou Enlai
Deng Xiaoping
questions.explanation: Students gathered to mourn Hu Yaobang, who died on 15 April 1989, and turned the mourning into demands for reform. Deng died in 1997 and Zhao in 2005; Zhou's death in 1976 had prompted the earlier Tiananmen Incident.

questions.stem: Which combination best summarises the reasons for the 1989 protests?
options: anger at inflation and official corruption, with demands for press freedom and dialogue
anger at the return of the communes, with demands for a return to Maoist policies
anger at Soviet troops on Chinese soil, with demands for war against the USSR
anger at the Special Economic Zones, with demands for the expulsion of all foreigners from China
questions.explanation: Students and later workers protested against corruption, inflation and privilege, and called for freedom of the press and for the government to talk with them. Workers' grievances over prices and job insecurity widened the movement.

questions.stem: Why did the visit of Mikhail Gorbachev to Beijing in May 1989 add to the pressure on the Chinese leadership?
options: Gorbachev cancelled the visit in protest, which ended the Sino-Soviet alliance
The world's media were in Beijing for the summit, and students occupied the square where he was to be welcomed
Gorbachev publicly demanded that Deng resign and hand power to the student leaders
Gorbachev brought Soviet troops with him to help the government clear the square
questions.explanation: The first Sino-Soviet summit since the split had brought foreign journalists to Beijing, and the occupation of the square embarrassed the leaders, who had to change the welcome ceremony. Martial law was declared on 20 May, soon after he left.

questions.stem: What do the different responses of Zhao Ziyang and Li Peng in May 1989 show about the CCP leadership?
options: It was divided: Zhao sought dialogue with the students, while Li backed martial law
It was united: both men visited the students and promised them free elections
It was powerless: neither man held office, and the army acted without orders
It was reformist: both men resigned rather than allow martial law to be declared in Beijing
questions.explanation: Zhao visited the hunger strikers in the square and opposed martial law; he was removed and kept under house arrest until his death. Premier Li Peng announced martial law, with the backing of Deng and the party elders.

questions.stem: What happened on the night of 3-4 June 1989 in Beijing?
options: The protesters left peacefully after the government agreed to all of their demands
The army joined the protesters and arrested Li Peng and the other party leaders
Police used only tear gas, and no deaths were reported anywhere in the city
The army forced its way into central Beijing and cleared the square, killing many civilians
questions.explanation: Troops fired on crowds blocking their way, especially on the avenues west of the square, and cleared the square by the morning of 4 June. The death toll has never been officially disclosed, and estimates range from hundreds to thousands.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the impact of June Fourth on China and its standing in the world?
options: China was expelled from the United Nations, and the party abandoned economic reform for a planned economy
The party introduced multiparty elections within a year to restore its standing with Western governments
Western governments quickly praised the crackdown and expanded arms sales to China in 1989
Western states imposed sanctions such as arms embargoes, while the party tightened political control but kept economic reform
questions.explanation: The USA and the European Community imposed arms embargoes and other sanctions, and China's image suffered badly. Zhao was replaced by Jiang Zemin, political control and censorship tightened, and after a pause economic reform resumed, speeding up after Deng's Southern Tour of 1992.
